workflow_hypothesis: Concurrent unsynchronized access to shared byte storage
pattern: Unsynchronized concurrent access to shared runtime state
description: Concurrent execution accesses shared object, interpreter, extension, iterator, cache, lifecycle, or resource state without a synchronization protocol that covers all conflicting operations.
precondition: The same mutable state, including state mutated lazily or during initialization, teardown, iteration, or caching, is reachable from multiple threads.
critical_operation: A thread reads, writes, initializes, advances, clears, or releases that shared state.
interference: Another thread concurrently performs a conflicting access to the same state without a common lock, atomic protocol, or lifetime handoff.
invalid_assumption: The implementation assumes that prior serialization, apparent read-only use, one-time initialization, or independent callers prevents overlap or makes ordinary field access safe.
failure: The conflicting accesses constitute a data race with undefined behavior; race instrumentation reports it, and some cases produce corrupted state, leaks, double release, crashes, or invalid results.
search_strategy: Audit shared fields read or written after releasing global or object-level serialization.
Require lazy cache and one-time initialization paths to use an atomic publication or a lock.
Check iterator advance, close, clear, and destruction paths for concurrent ownership and lifetime handoff.
Review extension and foreign-library callbacks for shared mutable context, configuration, and resource state.
Test concurrent getters, setters, initialization, finalization, and iteration under race detection.

evidence.supports: Concurrent iteration, cached metadata creation, and resource closure accessed shared iterator and entry state without sufficient coordination.
Allocation-related object state required thread-affine initialization to avoid concurrent unsafe state changes.
Concurrent access to a shared operating-system resource handle produced a race report.
Concurrent lazy creation and publication of a text representation raced with access to the same object state.
Concurrent readers and writers of callable dispatch metadata raced during invocation.
Attribute access and concurrent dictionary setup conflicted on shared object state.
Concurrent evaluation raced on a shared runtime signal-status field.
Concurrent hash caching performed an ordinary read and write of the same shared field.
Concurrent interning mutated shared text-object or intern-table state without complete synchronization.
Concurrent member retrieval and replacement conflicted on a shared object reference field.
A representation update raced with a consistency check reading the same text-object state.
Concurrent intern-table operations exposed unsynchronized shared interning state.
Subinterpreter concurrency exercises exposed races in shared interpreter-related state.
Concurrent type allocation accessed shared allocation-related state without adequate synchronization.
Thread-local-storage deletion raced with thread attachment over shared lifecycle state.
Concurrent extension use exposed races across reference, allocation, construction, operation, and interpreter-initialization state.
Concurrent executor activity exposed a race in thread-acquisition state.
Concurrent buffer export, release, and shared container access lacked a complete publication and lifetime protocol.
Even with global serialization enabled, operations releasing it allowed a shared resource handle to race.
Concurrent queue activity triggered a race report on shared synchronization-related state.
Daemon-thread shutdown overlapped with shared runtime state changes.
Finalization and a concurrently active daemon thread raced over interpreter lifecycle state.
Concurrent interpreter/module initialization raced while publishing shared module state.
A two-thread locking exercise exposed an unsynchronized conflicting access.
Concurrent execution in generated code caused a race that manifested as an invalid memory access.
Concurrent foreign-library binding operations raced on shared binding or library state.
Iterator metadata was read and updated concurrently without a sufficient atomic protocol.
Concurrent replacement and use of function metadata raced on shared function state.
Concurrent cryptographic-library use exposed a shared-state race.
Shared arithmetic-context flags were mutated non-atomically while concurrently accessed.
Concurrent callback-related cryptographic processing raced over shared data consumed by a foreign routine.
Concurrent thread-list traversal and thread attachment exposed shared interpreter-state races.
A concurrent callback scenario reproduced a race in shared data passed to a foreign routine.
Readers observed a mapping while its construction and resizing still mutated shared storage.
Inspection of thread exception state raced with concurrent thread attachment.
A configuration getter and setter concurrently read and wrote a shared debug flag.
Concurrent cryptographic test activity exposed shared memory races observable by race detection.
A collection of minimal concurrent reproducers documented recurring unsynchronized shared-state accesses in free-threaded execution.
A representation operation plainly read iterator state while another thread could update it.
Concurrent text-object operations raced on shared representation and lifetime state, including a crash manifestation.
Concurrent advancement of one iterator raced on its current-object field and could double release it.
Concurrent lazy name-cache initialization raced and could leak a losing cached value.
Sharing an iterator across threads allowed concurrent state updates and duplicate release of its referenced container.
Concurrent iterator advancement corrupted a shared cursor and could crash.
Concurrent sorting accessed mutable sequence state without a protocol preventing conflicting operations.
Concurrent reads and updates of function naming metadata raced on shared fields.

scope_note: This pattern is broader than shared byte storage: the evidence covers any shared mutable runtime state. It does not claim that all concurrent use is unsafe; it applies when conflicting accesses lack a common synchronization, atomic-publication, or lifetime-management protocol.
